references_named: George Berkeley, A Treatise Concerning the Principles of Human Knowledge (1710)
Ronald Knox, the 'tree in the quad' limerick
rationale: Strong in-DNA candidate. The browser-native CSS containment property is genuinely appropriated as readymade (P2) and its literal skip-render behavior enacts Berkeley's esse est percipi at the rendering layer (P1). The mechanism-as-argument is clean: the JavaScript only takes attendance; existence is delegated to a performance heuristic. Double-coding works at both depths (P7), the limerick rebuttal lands, and the chance/order axis (P5) is legible (numbered grid × thrown rectangles). The anti-pattern fallback (naive realist) is a witty second beat. Narrative placement is strong — it explicitly answers The Creative Act as a simpler, vendor-enforced counterpart.
reservations: Craft has a minor smell — the 'supported' detection is hand-wavy (it || true-falls through regardless of actual event support, so the JS claims to attach a handler that may never fire on engines lacking the event but reporting CSS support; effectively the support path may not behave as documented on every browser). Also, the painted compositions are visually thin — single-hue ground plus 1–3 rectangles is the absolute minimum to be a 'painting,' and P3's 'smallest build' arguably slides toward decorative-generative here without the visual specificity of a real art-historical referent. Nuance/Novelty still pass but the chance compositions don't earn their keep the way Maleglitch's format artifacts do.
revision_suggestion: Either deepen the per-canvas composition to borrow a more specific visual idiom (e.g., a named art-historical gesture re-thrown) so the chance side has bite, or honestly detect contentvisibilityautostatechange support (typeof fig.addEventListener check + a fallback census based on IntersectionObserver) so the mechanism's metaphysical claim isn't softened by a fudged feature-test.
